stdout_head:
Delonix Engine — a daemonless, rootless-first container & microVM engine (kernel-native, Rust). The open-source engine that powers Delonix.

Usage: delonix <COMMAND>

Common Commands:
  run              Run a container from an image (pulls it if missing)
  exec             Execute a command inside a running container
  ps               List containers [alias: ls]
  logs             Show the logs (detached containers)
  build            Build an image from a Dockerfile or Delonixfile
  pull             Pull an image from a registry
  push             Publish a local image to an OCI registry
  images           List local images
  apply            Converge a manifest — the canonical spelling of `stack apply`
  stack            Apply a whole manifest (`delonix-manifest.yaml`) — every Kind, in dependency order
  vm               Declarative microVMs: create/ls/start/stop/console
  cluster          Kubernetes clusters: `kubeadm` bootstrap, VM provisioning, manifest generation
  init             Start the right project for THIS directory

Management Commands:
  container        Containers: run/ps/stop/rm/exec/logs/update/describe
  image            OCI images: pull/ls/remove/export. `vm image <cmd>` for golden VM images
  pod              Real multi-container pods (N containers sharing a netns): create/logs/exec/cp/attach/port-forward
  workload         Unified compute layer over containers AND VMs: ls/stop/rm (ADR-0002)
  volume           Named volumes and bind mounts: create/ls/rm/inspect
  secret           Encrypted-at-rest secret vault — the producer of `run --secret`
  bucket           S3-compatible object stores (buckets): ls/inspect/rm
  network          User networks: ls/create/rm/inspect
  net              Low-level network/infra plumbing, grouped: netns/flow/ingress/egress/httproute/tunnel
  system           The engine itself: events, state and disk usage
  provider         What each provider can do, measured on this host against the capability catalog (ADR-0050)

title: `api-resources` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Every Kind this engine serves: plural, shortnames, apiVersion and form.

Read from the same registry the parser, the schema and the reconciler read — there is no second table to disagree with them. It answers «what can I write in a manifest, and what do I type after `explain`».

`FORM` is the column that cannot be guessed: it says whether a document of that Kind survives the load under its own name, which is why a `kind: Egress` never appears in a plan as `Egress`.

Usage: delonix api-resources [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -o, --output <OUTPUT>
          Output format: `table` (default) or `json` (ADR-0005)
          
          [default: table]
          [possible values: table, json]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # every Kind, with the plural and the shortnames a caller can type
  delonix api-resources

  # the stable half, for automation (ADR-0005)
  delonix api-resources -o json

  # what a Kind lowers to — why `kind: Egress` never shows up as `Egress`
  delonix api-resources | grep -- '->'

SEE ALSO:
  delonix explain · delonix manifest schema · delonix stack plan · delonix
  stack apply

  delonix › api-resources

title: `apply` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Converge a manifest — the canonical spelling of `stack apply`.

Promoted to the top because the verb belongs to the MANIFEST, not to one group: a file with a Network, a Volume and a Pod in it is not a «stack» operation any more than it is a «network» one.

Usage: delonix apply [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -f, --file <FILE>
          

      --name <NAME>
          Stack name to own the resources with (`delonix.io/stack`)

      --dry-run
          Print what would be applied, and apply nothing — exiting as the apply would refuse (5 for a resource another stack owns, DX-5601)

      --replace <Kind/name>
          Authorize the recreate of a resource whose cold field changed

      --reboot <Kind/name>
          Allow stopping and starting a resource whose change converges only across a reboot, keeping its disk (`Kind/name`, or `all`)

      --prune
          Remove what this stack owns and the manifest no longer declares

      --plan-digest <DIGEST>
          Apply only if this is still the plan: a `planDigest` from `stack plan -o json` (repeatable, one per network document). A network document whose digest, recomputed now, is not among them is a stale plan — refused before anything is written

      --plan <FILE>
          Apply a saved plan from `stack plan -o json`: its change digests gate the apply exactly as `--plan-digest` (ADR-0088 A5). `-f` stays the input

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # converge a manifest — creates, updates hot, and refuses a recreate
  delonix apply -f delonix-manifest.yaml

  # see it first, change nothing
  delonix apply -f delonix-manifest.yaml --dry-run

  # also remove what this stack owns and the file no longer declares
  delonix apply -f delonix-manifest.yaml --prune

SEE ALSO:
  delonix plan · delonix wait · delonix manifest validate · delonix stack
  destroy

  delonix › apply

Re-attach to a running container's output stream (output only).

Same log file `logs -f` reads. Unlike `docker attach`, this is OUTPUT-ONLY: a detached container's stdin has nowhere to go (this engine keeps no live conduit to it once started, unlike a persistent per-container shim) — `-i`/`--stdin` is refused with a clear error instead of silently doing nothing.

Usage: delonix attach [OPTIONS] <ID>

Arguments:
  <ID>
          

Options:

          Refused: stdin forwarding isn't supported (see the command's own doc above)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # re-attach to the output of a detached container (output only)
  delonix attach web

title: `backup` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Archives of ONE resource (container/pod/vm/stack): create, ls, inspect, restore, schedule, remove.

The archive carries the record and the DATA of the volumes it uses — not the image and not the rootfs, which `backup restore` derives by pulling. A VM is the exception: its overlay disk IS its state, so that one travels.

For the whole node — registries, secrets, cluster PKI, the event log — the command is `delonix system snapshot create`, which is a different scope and not a second door to this one.

Usage: delonix backup <COMMAND>

Inspect Commands:
  inspect   What an archive holds, without unpacking it
  ls        The archives in a directory

Configure Commands:
  create    Write an archive of one resource, now
  remove    Delete an archive
  restore   Put a resource back from an archive
  schedule  Keep archiving this resource on a systemd user timer

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # archive one resource, now
  delonix backup create container db

  # what archives exist
  delonix backup ls --from /srv/backups

  # put one back
  delonix backup restore container-db-20260811-205312.tar.gz

SEE ALSO:
  delonix backup create · delonix backup ls · delonix backup restore · delonix
  system snapshot

  delonix › backup

title: `backup create` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Write an archive of one resource, now

Usage: delonix backup create [OPTIONS] <KIND> <NAME>

Arguments:
  <KIND>
          What to back up

          Possible values:
          - container
          - pod
          - vm
          - stack
          - systemcontainer: A system container on a remote provider (`kind: SystemContainer`): the archive is taken and kept on the provider's storage, not in a file here

  <NAME>
          Its name

Options:
      --to <TO>
          Where the archive goes: a directory, or `volume:<name>` for a named volume (default: the current directory)
          
          [default: .]

      --keep <N>
          How many archives of this resource to keep (default: 7, or `--max-for-day` when scheduling)

      --dry-run
          Print what would be archived, without writing anything

      --quiesce
          Ask the guest agent to flush and freeze the filesystems first (VMs only; needs qemu-guest-agent inside the guest)

      --stop
          Stop the workload for the duration of the backup, instead of freezing it hot.
          
          Only worth it for an application that keeps state in memory and never writes it down: freezing gives a crash-consistent archive, which anything with a journal or a write-ahead log recovers from.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # the record and the volumes' data — not the image, which restore pulls back
  delonix backup create container db

  # somewhere that is not here (a directory, or a named volume on a NAS)
  delonix backup create container db --to volume:nas-backups

  # a RUNNING VM — the guest does not pause and its PID does not change
  delonix backup create vm dev --to /srv/backups

  # guest-filesystem consistency, if qemu-guest-agent is installed in it
  delonix backup create vm dev --quiesce --to /srv/backups

  # actually stop it, for an application that keeps state only in RAM
  delonix backup create container cache --stop --to /srv/backups

  # see

title: `backup restore` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Put a resource back from an archive

Usage: delonix backup restore [OPTIONS] <ARCHIVE>

Arguments:
  <ARCHIVE>
          The archive: a path, or the bare name of one in `--from`

Options:
      --kind <KIND>
          Refuse unless the archive holds this kind.
          
          Optional because the archive already SAYS what it holds, and the old `restore <kind> <archive>` made the caller repeat it. The guard the original argued for is kept as an opt-in assertion, and the kind is always printed — so a restore never silently does something other than what was typed.

          Possible values:
          - container
          - pod
          - vm
          - stack
          - systemcontainer: A system container on a remote provider (`kind: SystemContainer`): the archive is taken and kept on the provider's storage, not in a file here

      --from <FROM>
          Where to look for the archive when it is named rather than a path
          
          [default: .]

      --force
          Restore even when the live resource has data that is not in the archive

      --dry-run
          Print what would be restored, without touching anything

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # put the data back (refuses while it is running — that would corrupt it)
  delonix backup restore container-db-20260811-205312.tar.gz

  # stop it, restore, start it again
  delonix backup restore ./container-db-20260811-205312.tar.gz --force

  # from the directory the backups live in, by bare name
  delonix backup restore stack-loja-20260811-210000 --from /srv/backups

  # refuse unless it holds a VM — the archive already says, this asserts it
  delonix backup restore vm-dev-20260811-210109.tar.gz --kind vm

  # what it would touch, without touching it
  delonix backup restore vm-dev-20260811-210109.tar.gz --dry-run

SEE ALSO:
  delonix backup inspect · delonix system snapshot restore · delonix container
  start · delonix vm start

  delonix › backup › rest

Usage: delonix backup schedule [OPTIONS] <KIND> <NAME>

Arguments:

      --to <TO>
          Where the archive goes: a directory, or `volume:<name>` for a named volume (default: the current directory)
          
          [default: .]

      --keep <N>
          How many archives of this resource to keep (default: 7, or `--max-for-day` when scheduling)

      --dry-run
          Print what would be archived, without writing anything

      --quiesce
          Ask the guest agent to flush and freeze the filesystems first (VMs only; needs qemu-guest-agent inside the guest)

      --stop
          Stop the workload for the duration of the backup, instead of freezing it hot.
          
          Only worth it for an application that keeps state in memory and never writes it down: freezing gives a crash-consistent archive, which anything with a journal or a write-ahead log recovers from.

stdout_head:
Kubernetes clusters: `kubeadm` bootstrap, VM provisioning, manifest generation.

Idempotent `kubeadm` bootstrap over SSH (`kind: KubernetesCluster`), full VM provisioning, or generating a k8s manifest from a running container/pod (`cluster kube generate`).

Usage: delonix cluster <COMMAND>

Lifecycle Commands:
  backup      Back up etcd's keyspace to a local file (VM-provisioned clusters only)
  create      Create a local Kubernetes cluster **without a manifest and without Docker**
  destroy     Remove a cluster entirely — nodes, kubeconfig, `~/.kube/config` entry
  kubeadm     Provision VMs (golden VM image) + `kubeadm` bootstrap
  restore     Restore etcd's keyspace from a snapshot taken with `cluster backup`
  start       Start every node of a stopped kind-mode cluster back up
  stop        Stop every node of a kind-mode cluster at once — no rebuild, no state lost
  upgrade     Upgrade a `mode: ssh` cluster to a newer Kubernetes version, kubeadm-style

Create Commands:
  init        Initialize a project with the cluster manifests (kind/vm/ssh)

Interact Commands:
  drain       Cordon a node and evict its pods
  health      Is the control-plane answering, and is every node `Ready`?
  kubeconfig  Print a cluster's kubeconfig from the local cache (no live SSH)
  load        Load local images into a kind-mode cluster's nodes, **without a registry**
  ls          List this host's clusters — kind-mode AND VM-based
  uncordon    Mark a drained node schedulable again

Declarative Commands:
  apply       Apply the `kind: KubernetesCluster` document(s) of a manifest
  kube        Generate a Kubernetes manifest from a container/pod already running locally

Maintenance Commands:
  prune       Reclaim the state of clusters that have no nodes left

Clusters Commands:
  network     Inspect and prepare the pod-network profiles

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

title: `cluster backup` responde a --help

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Back up etcd's keyspace to a local file (VM-provisioned clusters only).

`etcd.mode: stacked` (the kubeadm default) only — `etcd.mode: external` is not supported yet, and is refused by name rather than attempted. Reads the control-plane's own `apiserver-etcd-client` certificate over SSH; nothing on the cluster is changed.

Usage: delonix cluster backup [OPTIONS] <NAME>

Arguments:
  <NAME>
          Cluster name

Options:
      --to <TO>
          Destination file. Omit = `<root>/clusters/<name>/etcd-snapshot-<unix-time>.db`

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # etcd's keyspace, to the default path under the cluster's own state
  # directory

title: `cluster destroy` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Remove a cluster entirely — nodes, kubeconfig, `~/.kube/config` entry.

Serves BOTH families: a kind-mode cluster, whose nodes are containers, and a VM-provisioned one (`cluster kubeadm` / `mode: vm`), whose nodes are VMs — its load balancer and etcd members included.

What becomes of the NETWORK is the one real difference, and the rule is the same in both families: whoever created it owns it. A kind-mode cluster's `dlx-<name>` was made FOR it and goes with it. A VM cluster built WITHOUT `--network` was given one of its own, named `<cluster>-<hash>`, and that one goes with it too. A network you named in `--network` is yours, and is left alone. Volumes are never touched either, on purpose, same as `docker`.

A cluster whose nodes are already gone is still removable by name: what gets collected is the state directory, the exported kubeconfig and the matching context — the same thing `cluster prune <name>` does.

Omitting the name resolves among KIND-MODE clusters only, so name a VM cluster explicitly. For a kind-mode cluster this is the same removal `delonix delete clusters <name>` already does (the generic kubectl-style verb this engine gives every Kind) — just the more discoverable spelling inside `cluster --help`, with a confirmation prompt `delete` does not have. For a VM-provisioned one it is the ONLY verb that tears the cluster down: `cmd_delete` hands straight to kind-mode's `delete` and has no VM branch at all.

Usage: delonix cluster destroy [OPTIONS] [NAME]

Arguments:
  [NAME]
          Cluster name. Omit when there is only one

Options:
  -f, --force
          Skip the confirmation prompt (REQUIRED when stdin is not a terminal)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

  # and the ~/.kube/config entry — volumes untouched
  delonix cluster destroy lab

  # entries go — so d

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Cordon a node and evict its pods.

The manual step before touching a control-plane/worker host (upgrade, maintenance, decommission). A pure Kubernetes API operation: talks to the apiserver through the CACHED kubeconfig (the same file `cluster kubeconfig` prints), needs no SSH and no container to exec into — unlike `health`, this works identically for every cluster family (`resolve_kubeconfig_name` already treats kind-mode and SSH/kubeadm clusters the same). Shells out to the system `kubectl`, the same "never reinvent an existing client" rule `remote::ssh_run` already follows for `ssh`.

Usage: delonix cluster drain [OPTIONS] <NODE>

Arguments:
  <NODE>
          Kubernetes node name, as `kubectl get nodes` shows it

Options:
      --name <NAME>
          Cluster name. Omit when there is only one cached

      --ignore-daemonsets
          Also evict DaemonSet-managed pods (they would otherwise block the drain)

      --delete-emptydir-data
          Also evict pods using an `emptyDir` volume (their data is lost)

      --force
          Evict pods not managed by a controller too (bare Pods)

      --timeout <TIMEOUT>
          Give up waiting for eviction after this long (a `kubectl` duration, e.g. `5m`)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # cordon a node and evict its pods before touching it — needs no SSH, just
  # the cached kubeconfig
  delonix cluster drain lab-w1 --name lab

  delonix cluster drain lab-w1 --name lab --delete-emptydir-data --force

title: `cluster prune` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Reclaim the state of clusters that have no nodes left.

A cluster exists as long as containers carry its label — `cluster ls` derives it that way instead of keeping a registry that could drift. So a cluster whose nodes went away by another route (`container rm`, `system prune`, a lost rootfs) leaves its directory, its exported kubeconfig and its `~/.kube/config` context behind, and nothing ever collects them.

That context is the reason this is not cosmetic: it still points at `127.0.0.1:<port>`, and by now that port may answer for something else.

**A cluster with nodes is never touched, stopped ones included** — for that there is `cluster destroy` (or `delete clusters <name>`, the same removal without the prompt), which takes a name on purpose.

With no NAMES this collects every orphan at once; naming one collects that one and leaves the others exactly as they are.

Usage: delonix cluster prune [OPTIONS] [NAMES]...

Arguments:
  [NAMES]...
          Orphans to collect (omit = every cluster with no nodes left)

Options:
  -f, --force
          Skip the confirmation prompt (REQUIRED when stdin is not a terminal)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # collect what clusters with no nodes left behind: their directory, their
  # exported kubeconfig, and the `~/.kube/config` context still pointing at a
  # port that may now answer for something else
  delonix cluster prune

  # just this one orphan, leaving every other leftover exactly as it is
  delonix cluster prune kambacode

  # in CI, where there is no terminal to confirm at
  delonix cluster prune -f

Upgrade a `mode: ssh` cluster to a newer Kubernetes version, kubeadm-style.

Mirrors kubeadm's own manual, one-node-at-a-time procedure — deliberately NOT an unattended whole-cluster cascade. With no NODE argument, upgrades the control-plane LEADER only (`spec.controlPlane.hosts[0]`, the one host `kubeadm upgrade apply` runs on); with `<NODE>`, upgrades that other control-plane or worker host (`kubeadm upgrade node`). Drains before and uncordons after each node automatically, unless `--no-drain`.

Usage: delonix cluster upgrade [OPTIONS] --to <TO> [NODE]

Arguments:
  [NODE]
          Upgrade this control-plane/worker host instead of the control-plane leader

Options:
  -f, --file <FILE>
          Manifest with the `kind: KubernetesCluster` document (default: `./delonix-manifest.yaml`)

      --to <TO>
          Target Kubernetes version, e.g. `1.32.1`

      --no-drain
          Skip the automatic drain/uncordon around the node's own upgrade

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # the control-plane leader first — kubeadm's own procedure runs `upgrade
  # apply` there
  delonix cluster upgrade -f cloud.yaml --to 1.32.1

  # then every other control-plane/worker, one at a time — `kubeadm upgrade
  # node`
  delonix cluster upgrade -f cloud.yaml --to 1.32.1 lab-w1

  # a control-plane that schedules nothing anyway: skip the automatic
  # drain/uncordon
  delonix cluster upgrade -f cloud.yaml --to 1.32.1 --no-drain

  delonix cluster health · delonix cluster backup

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Create a container from an image WITHOUT starting it — the engine's `docker create`.

The record is registered in `Created` state and the rootfs prepared, but no process runs; `container start <id>` launches it later from the same record. Takes every flag `run` does, and pulls the image if missing.

Usage: delonix container create [OPTIONS] <IMAGE>...

Arguments:
  <IMAGE>...
          Image (e.g. `alpine:3.19`), then the command + arguments (default: the image's ENTRYPOINT/CMD)

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

General:
  -d, --detach
          Run in the background and print the ID

  -i, --interactive
          Keep STDIN open (Docker/Podman `-i`); a daemonless foreground `run` already inherits it, so `-it` gives an interactive shell. See `docs/cli-stability.md`

  -t, --tty
          Allocate a TTY (Docker/Podman `-t`); a foreground `run` inherits the operator's terminal (no pty is synthesized when stdout is not one). See `docs/cli-stability.md`

      --name <NAME>
          Container name (default: `dlx-<id>`)

      --hostname <HOSTNAME>
          Hostname inside the container (UTS namespace + `/etc/hostname`). Default: the container name (docker `--hostname`)

  -u, --user <USER>
          Run the process as this user: `uid[:gid]` or `name[:group]` (docker `--user`). Names are resolved in the image's `/etc/passwd`/`/etc/group`

      --entrypoint <ENTRYPOINT>
          Override the image's ENTRYPOINT (COMMAND becomes the arguments to this binary; `--entrypoint ""` clears it and runs just the COMMAND)

  -w, --workdir <WORKDIR>

expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
**Reconfigure a RUNNING container without stopping it** — ports, volumes, and bandwidth cap.

Unlike docker (where changing a port or a volume forces recreating the container), here the dataplane doesn't belong to the process lifecycle: ports are DNAT/hostfwd in front of the network and volumes come in through the kernel's mount API (`open_tree`/`move_mount`) in the mount namespace of the already-live container. The PID doesn't change and the process is never interrupted.

For which NETWORKS the container is on, see `network connect`/`network disconnect` — Docker's own verb for that, kept apart from ports/ volumes/limits, which Docker cannot reconfigure hot at all.

The changes are persisted in the registry, so a later `container start` reproduces the new configuration, not the original.

Usage: delonix container update [OPTIONS] <ID>

Arguments:
  <ID>

stdout_head:
What the MACHINE changed since the last apply — the whole stack, no target named.

`stack plan` answers "what would an apply do", which mixes the edits someone just made to the FILE with the edits someone made to the NODE. This drops the manifest from the comparison and keeps the two faces that belong to the node: the spec stamped on each resource when it was last applied, and what it looks like now. Whatever differs happened outside the declarative path.

The manifest is OPTIONAL: on a node without the repo this still answers, and says out loud which Kinds it could not enumerate without the file.

          [possible values: table, json]

          Exit 2 when there IS drift (0 = none, 1 = error) — the `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` contract, for a CI drift gate

      --correct
          Re-apply the manifest to reconcile the drift away, instead of only reporting it (needs a manifest)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:

Writes one delimited block (`# BEGIN delonix <root> … # END`) pointing every name at `127.0.0.1` — the L7 proxy's published port is how the host reaches a workload on the SDN. EXAMPLES:
  # print the block first — the names it would publish, one per line
  delonix hosts sync --print

  # write it, and keep it current as containers are exposed and removed
  sudo delonix hosts sync

  # remove the block
  sudo delonix hosts sync --off

OCI images: pull/ls/remove/export. `vm image <cmd>` for golden VM images

Usage: delonix image <COMMAND>

Lifecycle Commands:
  pull          Pull an image from a registry
  push          Publish a local image to an OCI registry
  remove        Remove a local image [alias: rm]

Inspect Commands:
  attestations  List the attestations attached to an image in its registry
  describe      Human-readable detail of one or more images, `kubectl describe`-style
  diff          Show how two images differ at the layer level
  exists        Exit 0 if the image exists locally, 1 if not — prints nothing (`podman image exists`)
  history       Layers of an image (digest + size), from base to top
  inspect       Full detail of one or more images as a JSON array (`docker image inspect`)
  ls            List local images [alias: list]
  provenance    Print or attach the SLSA provenance a `build --provenance` cached
  sbom          The image's SBOM as an SPDX 2.3 document, not the table `scan --sbom` prints
  scan          SBOM + CVE scan of an image
  tree          Layer stack of one image, base to top, as an indented tree
  verify        Verify the cosign signature of a local image against a public key

Configure Commands:
  login         Authenticate to an OCI registry
  logout        Remove the stored credentials of a registry
  sign          Sign an image with cosign-compatible ECDSA-P256, publishing the signature next to it in the registry
  tag           Give another name/tag to a local image (copies nothing — it's just a new name for the same content)
  untag         Remove one name/tag from an image without deleting its content (`podman untag`)

Storage Commands:
  export        Export an OCI runtime bundle (rootfs + config.json) for `runc`/`crun`
  import        Create an image from a rootfs tarball (`docker import`)
  load          Load an image from an archive (the counterpart of `save`)
  save          Save an image to a portable archive (`docker save`'s counterpart)
  s

title: `image build` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Build an image from a Dockerfile or Delonixfile

Usage: delonix image build [OPTIONS] --tag <TAG> [CONTEXT]

Arguments:
  [CONTEXT]
          Build context (default: `.`) — root for `COPY`
          
          [default: .]

Options:
  -f, --file <FILE>
          Path of the Dockerfile (default: `<context>/Dockerfile`)

  -t, --tag <TAG>
          Tag of the resulting image (`repo:tag`)

      --build-arg <BUILD_ARG>
          Build-time variable (`KEY=VALUE`), repeatable — only takes effect for a name the Dockerfile actually declares with `ARG KEY[=default]` (an override with no matching `ARG` is silently ignored, same as Docker)

      --no-cache
          Bypasses the layer cache entirely (neither reads nor writes it) — same as Docker's `--no-cache`

      --secret <SECRET>
          `id=<name>,src=<path>` — a secret a `RUN --mount=type=secret,id=<name>` can bind-mount for the duration of that one instruction (never baked into a layer). Repeatable

      --platform <PLATFORM>
          `linux/<arch>` (e.g. `linux/arm64`) — cross-arch build. Resolves the correct-arch base image and stamps it into the result; actually running a foreign-arch `RUN` needs the host's own binfmt_misc/qemu-user-static already registered (not managed by delonix — a clear preflight error names the missing interpreter instead of a confusing mid-build failure)

      --target <TARGET>
          Name or index of a `FROM ... AS <name>` stage to stop the build at and package as the result, instead of the Dockerfile's own final stage. Only the stages the target itself needs (everything at or before it, in file order) are built — later stages are skipped entirely

      --provenance [<mode>]
          Emit SLSA v1 provenance for this build, cached next to the image (attach it to a registry later with `image provenance <ref> --attach`). `--provenance` or `--provenance=max` records build-arg values; `--provenance=min` withholds them (safe on any build). Off by default

  -h, --help
          Print h

expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Export an OCI runtime bundle (rootfs + config.json) for `runc`/`crun`

Usage: delonix image export [OPTIONS] <IMAGE> <DIR>

Arguments:
  <IMAGE>
          

  <DIR>
          

Options:
      --rootless
          Emit a ROOTLESS bundle: add a user namespace and the current user's uid/gid mappings (container root -> your uid, then the delegated subuids), so `runc`/`crun` run it without root. Without it the bundle has no mappings and only runs as real root (`runc` refuses it rootless with "requires user namespaces"). The mappings are specific to THIS user, so the bundle is tied to this host's `/etc/subuid`

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # an OCI runtime bundle (rootfs + config.json) that `runc` or `crun` runs
  # directly
  delonix image export alpine:latest /tmp/alpine-bundle

  # the directory you then hand to another OCI runtime — this is a bundle to
  # run, not an archive to ship
  delonix image export postgres:16 /tmp/pg-bundle

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Authenticate to an OCI registry.

Stores the credentials in `<root>/auth.json`, docker/podman format. The password ALWAYS comes from stdin — never from an argument (it would end up in the shell history and in /proc).

Usage: delonix image login [OPTIONS] --username <USERNAME> <REGISTRY>

Arguments:
  <REGISTRY>
          Registry (e.g. `ghcr.io`, `docker.io`)

Options:

      --password-stdin
          Read the password/token from stdin (the only supported way)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # authenticate to a registry — the token comes from stdin, never from the
  # argv, where it would land in the shell history and in /proc
  printf '%s' "$GITHUB_TOKEN" | delonix image login ghcr.io -u angolardevops --password-stdin

  # the same for Docker Hub
  printf '%s' "$DOCKERHUB_TOKEN" | delonix image login docker.io -u myuser --password-stdin

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
The image's SBOM as an SPDX 2.3 document, not the table `scan --sbom` prints.

`delonix build` writes this automatically for every image it commits that has a package database this scanner reads (`apk`/`dpkg`) — this just prints the cached file (instant). For a pulled or older image that never went through this engine's `build`, it computes and caches one on the spot.

Usage: delonix image sbom [OPTIONS] <IMAGE>

Arguments:
  <IMAGE>
          

Options:
      --attach
          Attach the SBOM to the image in its registry as an in-toto attestation (OCI 1.1 referrer, cosign/buildx-compatible), instead of only printing it. Requires a registry reference the image was pushed to

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # the SPDX document a `delonix build` already wrote for this image
  delonix image sbom myapp:v1

  # for a pulled image that never went through this engine's build
  delonix image sbom postgres:16

  # attach the SBOM to the image in its registry as an in-toto attestation
  delonix image sbom ghcr.io/ngolacloud/app:1.2.0 --attach

  delonix image scan · delonix build · delonix image sign · delonix image
  attestations

title: `image scan` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
SBOM + CVE scan of an image.

Reads the layers from the CAS, without running anything. Pulls the image if missing. See `--sbom`, `--fail-on`, `--update`.

Usage: delonix image scan [OPTIONS] [IMAGE]

Arguments:
  [IMAGE]
          Image to scan (optional with `--update`)

Options:
      --sbom
          List the SBOM (installed packages) instead of scanning

      --fail-on <SEV>
          Fail (exit 1) if there are vulnerabilities >= this severity (low|medium|high|critical) — gate for CI

      --policy <FILE>
          Gate on a declarative policy file (JSON: `fail_on`, `ignore` waiver list, `ignore_unfixed`). Richer CI gate than `--fail-on`; takes precedence over it. Exits 1 on failure

      --compare-to <IMAGE>
          Report the vulnerability delta against another image (added/removed CVEs), like `docker scout compare`, instead of the dashboard

      --update
          Sync the CVE feed to the local database (used afterwards by each scan)

      --feed <URL|FILE>
          Feed source for `--update`: URL or file (or $DELONIX_ADVISORY_FEED)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # the CVEs of an image, read from the layers on disk — nothing is executed
  delonix image scan postgres:16

  # the installed packages (SBOM) instead of the findings
  delonix image scan --sbom nginx

  # a CI gate: exit 1 if anything high or worse is found
  delonix image scan --fail-on high ghcr.io/ngolacloud/app:1.2.0

  # refresh the local feed first — a scan is only as fresh as the database
  # behind it
  delonix image scan --update

SEE ALSO:
  delonix image describe · delonix image pull · delonix image verify

  delonix › image › scan

Score a `docker-compose.yml` against what this engine serves.

Reads the file and reports every key it uses: served, refused with a reason, or missing (with the engine's equivalent command where there is one). Nothing is created, pulled or run.

Only compose files today, and that is a measurement and not an oversight: the Compose Specification's key list was measured against the client that implements it, so the third state has a real denominator.   -h, --help

stdout_head:
Raw packet capture on a container's SDN interface, via the host's own `tcpdump`.

Runs `tcpdump` INSIDE the container's netns (the same `join_argv` prefix `--net <network>` uses to enter one), never a second capture engine. Containers only in this version — a pod member shares its pod's netns and is refused, pointing at the pod's name.

Usage: delonix net capture [OPTIONS] --write <WRITE> <CONTAINER>

Arguments:
  <CONTAINER>
          Container to capture (must be attached to a custom network — `--net host`/`none` have no netns of their own to enter)

Options:
  -i, --iface <IFACE>
          Interface inside the container's netns
          
          [default: eth0]

  -w, --write <WRITE>
          Where to write the capture: a file path, or `-` for stdout

  -c, --count <COUNT>
          Stop after this many packets

      --duration <DURATION>
          Stop after this many seconds (a real `SIGINT`, same as Ctrl-C — ignored if `--count` is reached first)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # write a pcap file, stop after 100 packets
  delonix net capture web -w out.pcap -c 100

  # stream straight into Wireshark for 30s

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Publish a host port to the container (DNAT through the ingress)

Usage: delonix net ingress publish <CONTAINER> <SPEC>

Arguments:
  <CONTAINER>
          Container to govern. Must be on the SDN (`--net <network>`)

  <SPEC>
          `[hostIp:]hostPort:containerPort[/tcp|udp]` or just `port`. SAFE BY DEFAULT: without `hostIp` the port binds to `127.0.0.1` only — reachable from the host itself, NOT from another machine. Name the address to widen it: `0.0.0.0:5070:5070/udp` (every interface), `192.168.1.10:8080:80` (one), or the libvirt gateway to reach it from VMs (see `delonix vm reach`). The resolved address is RECORDED, so it survives a `container start`

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # host 8080 onto the container's 80
  delonix net ingress publish web 8080:80

  # the same number on both sides
  delonix net ingress publish web 8443

  # a UDP service — rootless cannot bind host ports below 1024, so publish
  # high and let a proxy own :53 if you need it
  delonix net ingress publish dns 5353:53/udp

  # reachable from OTHER machines: without an address the port binds to
  # 127.0.0.1 alone
  delonix net ingress publish sip 0.0.0.0:5070:5070/udp

  # reachable from the VMs on a libvirt network, and from nowhere else — see
  # `delonix vm reach`
  delonix net ingress publish api 192.168.122.1:8080:80

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Reclaim infra left behind by state roots that no longer exist.

`down` tears the infra down BY PIDFILE, and the pidfiles live inside `$DELONIX_ROOT/ingress/`. Delete the root — a test harness cleaning up, a `/tmp` root swept by the system — and the pin, the control process and the slirp keep running with no name any command can reach. This finds them by asking `/proc` instead, and never touches a root that still exists, this one least of all.

Usage: delonix net netns gc [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -f, --force
          Terminate them. Without this, the sweep only reports

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # what is abandoned, and nothing else — the default only reports
  delonix net netns gc

  # reclaim it: pin, control process and slirp of every state root that no
  # longer exists
  delonix net netns gc --force

title: `network ipam prune` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Reclaim leases with no live container.

The fix `network diagnose`'s address-registry finding points at. Safe under load, same shape as `system prune`: a lease first seen orphaned is only a CANDIDATE, and is reclaimed on a LATER run that still finds it orphaned past the grace window — never on the pass that first notices it, so a container mid-creation never loses the address it just allocated. Runs under the allocator's own lock.

Options:
      --dry-run
          Preview what would be reclaimed, without touching the registry

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # preview what would be reclaimed, without touching the registry
  delonix network ipam prune --dry-run

  # reclaim leases with no live container, past the grace window
  delonix network ipam prune

The CERT is the trust anchor you pass to every server as `serve node-api --tls-client-ca`; the KEY stays with the enrollment authority (`serve node-enroll`) and no node-API server ever holds it (ADR-0097).

      --out-key <PEM>

title: `node-enroll` responde a --help

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Enroll this host as a fleet member: one-time token → CSR → short client cert.

Generates a key pair and a CSR, exchanges a one-time token at an enrollment authority (`serve node-enroll`) pinned to the node CA, and writes the short-lived client certificate the node API (ADR-0096) then accepts (ADR-0097). NOT stable: see `docs/cli-stability.md`.

Usage: delonix node-enroll [OPTIONS] --server <SERVER> --ca <PEM> --token <TOKEN> --cn <CN>

Options:
      --server <SERVER>
          The enrollment authority address: `host:port` or `tcp://host:port`

      --ca <PEM>
          The node CA certificate (PEM) to PIN for the authority's server identity — this is what stops a man-in-the-middle from harvesting the token

      --token <TOKEN>
          The one-time enrollment token

      --cn <CN>
          The subject common name = this member's identity in its certificate

      --san <SAN>
          A subject alternative name (IP or DNS) for the client certificate. Repeatable; usually unnecessary for a client identity

      --out-key <PEM>
          Where to write the generated private key (PEM, `0600`) — it never leaves this host
          
          [default: client.key]

      --out-cert <PEM>
          Where to write the issued client certificate (PEM)
          
          [default: client.crt]

      --out-ca <PEM>
          Where to also write the CA bundle the authority returned (PEM)

      --force
          Overwrite existing output files

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # enroll this host: generate a key and CSR, spend a one-time token, write
  # `client.key`/`client.crt`
  delonix node-enroll --server tcp://10.0.0.1:7443 --ca node-ca.crt --token s3cret --cn worker-7

title: `secret create` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Create a secret from literals and/or a `.env` file.

Refuses if the name already exists — pass `--force` to replace it, or use `secret set` to add/update keys instead.

Usage: delonix secret create [OPTIONS] <NAME>

Arguments:
  <NAME>
          

Options:
      --from-literal <FROM_LITERAL>
          `KEY=value` pair. Repeatable

      --from-env-file <FROM_ENV_FILE>
          Load `KEY=value` lines from a file (e.g. `.env`), or `-` to read them from stdin (the value never touches argv/process list)

      --from-env <FROM_ENV>
          Take the value from an environment VARIABLE: `--from-env DB_PASSWORD` stores `$DB_PASSWORD` under that name, `--from-env password=<REDACTED> under `password`. Repeatable. The value never appears in argv, unlike `--from-literal`

  -f, --force
          Replace an EXISTING secret instead of refusing. Without it, `create` only creates — the same guarantee `kubectl create secret`/`docker secret create` give; use `secret set` to add or update keys of one that already exists without this flag

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # from literal pairs — quick, but the value lands in your shell history
  delonix secret create db-pass --from-literal PASSWORD=<REDACTED>

  # from a `.env` file, every key at once
  delonix secret create db-pass --from-env-file .env

  # from stdin — the dry form: the value touches neither argv nor the history
  printf 'PASSWORD=<REDACTED> | delonix secret create db-pass --from-env-file -

SEE ALSO:
  delonix secret set · delonix secret ls · delonix secret apply · delonix
  container run

stdout_head:
Rotate one key's VALUE to a fresh random one.

Distinct from `rotate-key`: this replaces a single key's value with new random bytes, and touches nothing else in the secret. Meant for values this engine or the operator mints themselves (a database password, an HMAC signing key) — an externally-issued credential (a third-party API key) still has to be rotated at the issuer and landed here with `secret set`.

Usage: delonix secret rotate [OPTIONS] <NAME> <KEY>

Arguments:
  <NAME>
          

  <KEY>
          

Options:
      --length <LENGTH>
          Random bytes to generate (hex-encoded, so the stored value is twice this many characters)
          
          [default: 32]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # mint a fresh random value for one key, keeping the rest of the secret
  # untouched
  delonix secret rotate db-pass PASSWORD

  # a longer generated value — the stored string is twice this many hex
  # characters
  delonix secret rotate db-pass PASSWORD --length 48

title: `serve cri` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Serve the CRI endpoint (`runtime.v1`) on a unix socket — replaces containerd/CRI-O for a kubelet

Usage: delonix serve cri [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --addr <ADDR>
          Socket address (default: `$DELONIX_CRI_ADDR` or `unix:///run/delonix-cri.sock`)

      --cap-ceiling <LIST>
          Node-level UPPER BOUND on container capabilities, whatever the kubelet asks for: a comma-separated list of names (`NET_ADMIN`, `CAP_CHOWN`), `none`, `default` (the engine's default set, and what an unset value means), `default,<extra>...`, or `all` (no bound, only when asked for). Overrides `$DELONIX_CRI_CAP_CEILING`. Bounds capabilities ONLY — a privileged pod still gets unconfined seccomp

      --cap-ceiling-mode <MODE>
          What to do with a pod that asks for more than `--cap-ceiling`: `reject` (default, fails CreateContainer so the kubelet reports it) or `clamp` (reduce to the ceiling and log a warning). Overrides `$DELONIX_CRI_CAP_CEILING_MODE`

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # the CRI endpoint on the default socket — point the kubelet's
  # `--container-runtime-endpoint` at it
  delonix serve cri

  # a socket of your own
  delonix serve cri --addr unix:///run/delonix-cri.sock

  # a node-level bound on capabilities that holds even if the admission chain
  # is misconfigured
  delonix serve cri --cap-ceiling default,NET_ADMIN

  # clamp instead of refusing, for a node whose PodSpecs you cannot change
  # today
  delonix serve cri --cap-ceiling default --cap-ceiling-mode clamp

SEE ALSO:
  delonix serve api · delonix cluster kubeadm · delonix container run

  delonix › serve › cri

Serve the NODE API (gRPC + HTTP/JSON of `delonix.node.v1`) on a unix socket.

The versioned node contract (ADR-0040): node info, health, capacity, providers, events, operations, networks, volumes and virtual machines, with `GET /openapi.json` rendered at `GET /docs` and `GET /redoc`. It is not a daemon: `--install-units` writes a systemd socket unit that starts it on the first connection, and it exits after `--idle-timeout` with nothing open.

Usage: delonix serve node-api [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --addr <ADDR>
          Socket address: a unix path (`unix:///run/delonix-node.sock`, the default, or `$DELONIX_NODE_API_ADDR`) or a TCP address (`tcp://host:port`). A `tcp://` address serves mutual TLS and requires `--tls-cert`/`--tls-key`/`--tls-client-ca`

      --idle-timeout <DURATION>
          Exit after this long with no connection open and no operation running: `120`, `90s`, `5m`, `0` for never. Default: 300s when started by socket activation, never otherwise

      --tls-cert <PEM>
          TLS: the server certificate chain (PEM path). Required for a `tcp://` address (ADR-0096); together with `--tls-key` and `--tls-client-ca`. Overrides `$DELONIX_NODE_API_TLS_CERT`

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Serve the ENROLLMENT AUTHORITY (ADR-0097): trade a one-time token for a short client cert.

A server-TLS-only endpoint (`POST /v1/enroll`) that signs a member's CSR with the node CA key it holds (`--ca-key`) and returns a short-lived client certificate. The member pins the node CA; the token authenticates it. This is NOT a node-API server and never holds a node's data — it holds the CA key, so run it deliberately, not by socket activation.

Usage: delonix serve node-enroll [OPTIONS] --addr <ADDR>

Options:
      --addr <ADDR>
          Address to listen on: `tcp://host:port` (server-authenticated TLS)

      --ca-key <PEM>
          The node CA private key (PEM path) — used to sign CSRs and the authority's own cert
          
          [default: node-ca.key]

      --ca-cert <PEM>
          The node CA certificate (PEM path) — echoed to members in the response
          
          [default: node-ca.crt]

      --cn <CN>
          The CA subject common name (must match `node-ca init --cn`)
          
          [default: delonix-node-ca]

      --token <TOKEN>
          A valid one-time enrollment token. Repeatable

      --token-file <FILE>
          A file of one-time tokens, one per line (`#` comments and blanks skipped)

      --san <SAN>
          A SAN (IP/DNS) for the authority's own server certificate — the address members reach it at. Repeatable; 127.0.0.1 and localhost are always included

      --cert-ttl <DURATION>
          Lifetime of the client certificates issued: `60s`, `30m`, `1h`. Default 1h
          
          [default: 1h]

      --server-cert <PEM>
          An explicit server certificate (PEM path) instead of auto-issuing one from the CA

      --server-key <PEM>
          The explicit server certificate's key (PEM path); required with `--server-cert`

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Applies all the manifest Kinds (Network → Volume → Image → Vm → Container)

Usage: delonix stack apply [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --name <NAME>
          Stack name (the owner stamped on every resource). Default: a `kind: Stack`'s name, else the manifest's directory

  -f, --file <FILE>
          

      --dry-run
          Don't apply anything — print the full manifest with every default filled in, then plan it against the machine and refuse what `apply` would refuse, with the same exit (like `kubectl apply --dry-run=server -o yaml`). A resource another stack owns exits 5 (DX-5601). Nothing is applied; `manifest render` is the offline view

      --replace <KIND/NAME>
          Authorize DESTROYING and recreating a resource whose change does not converge live: `--replace <Kind>/<name>` (repeatable), or `--replace all`. Without it, `apply` refuses and changes nothing. A `<Kind>/<name>` also recreates that resource when the plan shows no change for it (a field the plan does not compare, like `env`)

      --reboot <KIND/NAME>
          Authorize STOPPING and starting a resource whose change converges only across a reboot, keeping its disk (ADR-0012): `--reboot <Kind>/<name>` (repeatable), or `--reboot all`. Without it, `apply` refuses and changes nothing. A stopped VM needs no authorisation

      --prune
          Also REMOVE what this stack owns and the manifest no longer declares. Never happens without this flag

      --plan-digest <DIGEST>
          Apply only if this is still the plan: the `planDigest` of each change from `stack plan -o json` (repeatable). A change whose digest, recomputed now, is not among them is a stale plan — refused before anything is written

      --plan <FILE>
          Apply a saved plan from `stack plan -o json`: its change digests gate the apply exactly as `--plan-digest` (ADR-0088 A5). `-f` stays the input

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

title: `stack describe` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Stack detail in `kubectl describe` style.

Each resource DECLARED in the manifest and whether or not it is present on the machine.

**The stack has no state of its own** — there is no registry of "stacks", only a manifest and the resources it creates. That is why this `describe` always starts from the file and goes to confirm each resource against the respective store, instead of inventing a new registry that would drift out of sync (the same reason `cluster ls` derives its state from the container labels).

The column that matters is PRESENCE: an `apply` is fail-fast and without rollback, so a half-applied stack is a normal state and this is exactly what it shows.

Usage: delonix stack describe [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -f, --file <FILE>
          

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # each declared resource in kubectl-describe style, confirmed against its
  # store
  delonix stack describe -f prod.yaml

  # after an apply that died halfway, see exactly what did get created
  delonix stack describe

SEE ALSO:
  delonix stack ls · delonix stack plan · delonix container describe

title: `stack history` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
What this stack applied, and when (ADR-0019).

One revision per `apply` that asked for a change, failed ones included and marked — after an incident the question is what the machine was ASKED to do, not what it managed to do. An apply with nothing to change (what left the manifest, without `--prune`, is kept) writes none. `--show <n>` prints that revision's rendered manifest.

This is a RECORD, never a source of truth: nothing here is read to decide what exists. Delete `<root>/stacks/` and every other stack command keeps working — only the history is lost.

Usage: delonix stack history [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --name <NAME>
          Stack name. Default: a `kind: Stack`'s name, else the manifest's directory

  -f, --file <FILE>
          

      --show <N>
          Print the rendered manifest of revision N instead of the list

  -o, --output <OUTPUT>
          Output format: `table` (default) or `json` (ADR-0005) — `json` carries the FULL error of a failed revision, which the table truncates
          
          [default: table]
          [possible values: table, json]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # what this stack applied, and when
  delonix stack history -f prod.yaml

  # the rendered manifest of one revision, to diff against today's
  delonix stack history -f prod.yaml --show 3

  # machine-readable, and the only form carrying the FULL error of a failed
  # apply

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Shows what an `apply` WOULD change, without changing anything.

Compares the manifest against the machine and against the last spec this stack applied (a three-way diff, so a field a human set by hand is left alone while a field removed from the manifest is reverted). With the manifest unchanged, whatever it prints IS drift.

Usage: delonix stack plan [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -f, --file <FILE>
          

      --name <NAME>
          Stack name (owner of the resources). Default: a `kind: Stack`'s name, else the manifest's directory

  -o, --output <OUTPUT>
          Output format: `table` (default) or `json` (ADR-0005)
          
          [default: table]
          [possible values: table, json]

      --detailed-exitcode
          Exit 2 when there are changes, 5 when the plan holds a conflict `stack apply` would refuse (0 = none, 1 = error) — the `terraform plan -detailed-exitcode` contract, for a CI drift gate

      --prune
          Plan what `stack apply --prune` would do: what this stack owns and the manifest no longer declares counts as a change, to remove. Without it, it is listed as KEPT — `apply` removes nothing without `--prune` — and does not count for `--detailed-exitcode`

      --fields
          Print WHICH fields the plan compares, per Kind, and exit. Answers "why is my change not showing up?" without reading the source

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # what an apply would change — the machine is not touched
  delonix stack plan -f prod.yaml

  # a drift gate in CI: exit 2 means the machine no longer matches the file
  delonix stack plan -f prod.yaml --detailed-exitcode

  # the same gate when the pipeline applies with --prune: what left the file
  # counts as a removal
  delonix stack plan -f prod.yaml --prune --detailed-exitcode

  # machine-readable, for a bot to comment on a pull request
  delonix stack plan -f prod.yaml -o json

title: `stack prune` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Remove what this stack owns and the manifest no longer declares.

The pruning half of `apply --prune`, on its own: nothing is created, nothing is converged, and a resource whose declaration is still in the file is left exactly as it is. The use it exists for is the one `apply --prune` cannot serve — dropping a resource from the manifest and collecting it WITHOUT re-running everything else the stack declares.

Ownership is the `delonix.io/stack` label, same as `destroy`: a resource created by hand, or belonging to another stack, is never a candidate.

Like `destroy` — and unlike `container prune`/`vm prune` — this asks nothing at a terminal. The manifest is the authorization: what goes is exactly what you deleted from a file you wrote. `--dry-run` is the preview.

Usage: delonix stack prune [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -f, --file <FILE>
          

      --name <NAME>
          Stack name (owner of the resources). Default: a `kind: Stack`'s name, else the manifest's directory

      --dry-run
          List what would be removed, and remove nothing

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # remove what this stack owns and the manifest no longer declares, WITHOUT
  # re-running everything else the file declares
  delonix stack prune -f prod.yaml

  # see the list first and remove nothing
  delonix stack prune -f prod.yaml --dry-run

SEE ALSO:
  delonix stack apply · delonix stack destroy · delonix stack plan · delonix
  stack ls

title: `stack rollback` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Re-apply a recorded revision (ADR-0019).

A rollback IS an apply: it replays the manifest of revision N through the same path a normal apply takes, and gets a revision of its own. It is not a time machine, and the differences are printed before anything runs — what was created after N stays unless `--prune`, and data that was deleted does not come back.

Usage: delonix stack rollback [OPTIONS] --to <N>

Options:
      --to <N>
          Revision to replay. `stack history` lists them

      --name <NAME>
          Stack name. Default: a `kind: Stack`'s name, else the manifest's directory

  -f, --file <FILE>
          

      --dry-run
          Show the plan and change nothing

      --replace <KIND/NAME>
          Authorize destroying and recreating a resource whose change does not converge live — same meaning as in `apply`

      --reboot <KIND/NAME>
          Authorize stopping and starting a resource whose change converges only across a reboot — same meaning as in `apply`

      --prune
          Also REMOVE what this stack owns and the replayed revision does not declare — this is what makes a rollback actually undo a creation

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # see what going back to revision 3 would change, and change nothing
  delonix stack rollback --to 3 --dry-run

  # replay revision 3
  delonix stack rollback --to 3

  # and also remove what was created after it — without this, a rollback
  # undoes no creation
  delonix stack rollback --to 3 --prune

SEE ALSO:
  delonix stack history · delonix stack apply · delonix stack plan · delonix
  stack destroy

title: `system prune` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Reclaim space taken by what nothing uses any more.

Removes stopped containers, unused images, CAS blobs nobody references, empty cgroups and — the biggest space saver — **orphan container directories** (from nodes/containers that died abruptly without `rm`, with no registry entry).

Usage: delonix system prune [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -f, --force
          Skip the confirmation prompt (REQUIRED when stdin is not a terminal)

  -a, --all
          Also remove unused images that DO have a tag (not just the dangling ones)

      --build-cache
          Also reclaim the ENTIRE build cache now, ignoring the 7-day last-use TTL that `prune` otherwise honours. Implied by `--all`.
          
          The build cache is rebuildable content and is often the single biggest reclaimable block, yet the TTL can hold a day-old 6 GiB out of reach: this is the on-demand counterpart of deleting the `build-cache/` directory by hand, which `system df` used to be the only way to suggest. The next build simply repopulates what it needs.

      --auto
          SCHEDULED mode: reclaim only when the disk is at or above `--threshold`, and do nothing at all below it.
          
          This is the flag that makes `system prune` safe to put in a timer. Below the threshold it exits 0 having changed nothing, and that is SUCCESS, not a no-op to be fixed: pruning every night by habit deletes images that get pulled again in the morning, which costs bandwidth and start-up time and reclaims nothing that was a problem.
          
          It implies `--force` — an unattended sweep has nobody to answer a prompt — and it never touches volumes (see `volume prune`).

      --threshold <THRESHOLD>
          Occupancy percentage at or above which `--auto` acts.
          
          Measured the way `df` measures it, on the filesystem holding the engine's state. Keep it BELOW the threshold of whatever alerts on the same disk: the GC has to act before someone is woken up, and with equal numbers the alert alw

title: `system regulate` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Give the contended CPU back to the workloads that are waiting for it.

Reads pressure, finds the workload CAUSING it (the biggest consumer — not the one with the highest stall, which is the victim), halves its `cpu.weight`, and gives it back when the contention passes. `cpu.weight` is a SHARE, not a cap: with nothing to compete against, a throttled workload still gets the whole machine. Nothing is ever killed or paused.

Prints the plan and changes nothing unless `--apply` is given.

Usage: delonix system regulate [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --apply
          Carry the plan out. Without it this is a report

      --once
          One decision and exit, for a systemd timer or a cron

      --interval <INTERVAL>
          Seconds between decisions when looping
          
          [default: 30]

      --floor <FLOOR>
          Never take a workload's `cpu.weight` below this
          
          [default: 20]

      --install-timer
          Install a systemd timer that runs one decision every `--interval` seconds, and exit.
          
          A timer and not a daemon, on purpose: this engine is daemonless by design, and a resident process would need its own ADR. What the timer fixes is the other half of the problem — a regulator nobody starts regulates nothing.

      --uninstall-timer
          Remove the timer this command installed, and exit

  -o, --output <OUTPUT>
          Output format: `table` (default) or `json` (ADR-0005)
          
          [default: table]
          [possible values: table, json]

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # see which workload is causing the contention, and what would be done about
  # it
  delonix system regulate --once

  # actually do it — halve the culprit's cpu share, and give it back when it
  # passes
  delonix system regulate --apply

  # one decision and exit, for a systemd timer
  delonix system regulate --apply --once

SEE ALSO:
  delonix system resources · delonix system thermal ·

title: `system resources` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
How much this host has, how much the engine can actually enforce, and what is under pressure right now.

`info` says whether there IS delegation and `doctor` says whether the prerequisites are met. Neither says WHICH controllers were delegated, and that is the question behind a whole class of silent failures: a `--cpuset-cpus` or an `--io-max` on a host without those controllers is parsed, accepted, and ignored, with the container running unbounded and nothing anywhere saying so. This names the ignored flags. Read-only.

Usage: delonix system resources [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -o, --output <OUTPUT>
          Output format: `table` (default) or `json` (ADR-0005)
          
          [default: table]
          [possible values: table, json]

      --strict
          Exit non-zero on a `config` or `capacity` finding, for a fleet gate.
          
          Never on a `load` one: pressure is what this minute looks like, and a gate that goes red because somebody ran a build teaches everyone to ignore it.

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # capacity, what the engine can actually enforce, and what is stalled right
  # now
  delonix system resources

  # name the flags this host accepts and silently ignores
  delonix system resources

  # machine-readable, for a capacity dashboard or a gate
  delonix system resources -o json

SEE ALSO:
  delonix system setup · delonix system info · delonix system doctor · delonix
  container run

  delonix › system › resources

title: `system setup` responde a --help

source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Diagnose — and, with `--delegate`, fix — cgroup delegation.

It is the prerequisite for `--memory`/`--cpus` to mean anything. Without it the flags are ACCEPTED and INERT: the container runs with no limit at all. That is the failure mode this command exists for, and it is invisible without asking.

Usage: delonix system setup [OPTIONS]

Options:

          Apply the fix instead of only reporting it. Writing the system-wide drop-in needs root; the per-session remedy never does

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # diagnose cgroup delegation — without it --memory and --cpus are accepted
  # and inert
  delonix system setup

  # apply the fix instead of only reporting it (the system-wide drop-in needs
  # root)
  delonix system setup --delegate

title: `system snapshot` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Point-in-time capture of this node's whole state — `create` saves it into one archive, `restore` puts it back.

Same vocabulary as `vm snapshot`/`volume snapshot`: a point-in-time capture, scoped here to the whole node instead of one resource. Renamed from the top-level `system backup`/`system restore` (which collided by name, not by scope, with the unrelated `backup` group — one resource's data, never the node's) — the two scopes stay exactly as separate as they always were, only the shared word is gone.

Usage: delonix system snapshot <COMMAND>

Configure Commands:
  create   Save this node's state into one archive
  restore  Put a node's state back from a `system snapshot create` archive

Options:
  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # the registries, IPAM, secrets and PKI — everything that cannot be rebuilt
  delonix system snapshot create

  # put the state back (refuses while a container or VM is still running)
  delonix system snapshot restore node-a.tar.gz

SEE ALSO:
  delonix system snapshot create · delonix system snapshot restore · delonix
  backup · delonix vm snapshot

  delonix › system › snapshot

title: `system snapshot create` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Save this node's state into one archive.

By default it packs what CANNOT be reconstructed: the registries, IPAM, secrets, `auth.json`, cluster PKI, HTTPRoute config and the event log. The heavy, re-obtainable areas are opt-in, and the live plumbing of a running node (pidfiles, sockets, locks) never travels — a resurrected `holder.pid` makes the engine report a holder that does not exist.

Usage: delonix system snapshot create [OPTIONS]

Options:
  -o, --output <OUTPUT>
          Where to write the archive (default: `delonix-backup-<UTC>.tar.gz` in the current directory). Always created 0600

      --volumes
          Also pack the volumes' DATA, via the same mapped snapshot `volumes snapshot` uses. This is the only area that can be hundreds of GiB

      --images
          Also pack the OCI images (blobs, layers and index) — content-addressed cache that a registry can serve again

      --vm-images
          Also pack the VM disk images (gigabytes of qcow2 that `vm pull` re-fetches). Their metadata always travels

      --include-master-key
          Also pack the vault MASTER KEY. Without it the secrets restore onto another node as bytes that never decrypt; with it, the archive IS the vault

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # the registries, IPAM, secrets and PKI — everything that cannot be rebuilt
  delonix system snapshot create

  # name the file yourself
  delonix system snapshot create -o /mnt/nas/node-a.tar.gz

  # take the volumes' data with it (this is the part that can be hundreds of
  # GiB)
  delonix system snapshot create --volumes

  # to rebuild a node from scratch: without the key the secrets never decrypt
  # there
  delonix system snapshot create --volumes --include-master-key

SEE ALSO:
  delonix system snapshot restore · delonix volume snapshot · delonix system
  df · delonix secret ls

  delonix › system › snapshot › create

title: `system snapshot restore` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Put a node's state back from a `system snapshot create` archive.

Destructive on purpose: the covered set becomes exactly what the archive holds. It verifies the whole archive BEFORE touching anything, refuses a format it does not know, refuses to run over live workloads without `--force`, and proves afterwards that the restored secrets decrypt.

Usage: delonix system snapshot restore [OPTIONS] <ARCHIVE>

Arguments:
  <ARCHIVE>
          The archive written by `system snapshot create`

Options:
  -f, --force
          Restore even with containers/VMs still running (their registry is replaced underneath them)

      --dry-run
          Say what would change and stop, without writing anything

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # what it would change, without writing anything
  delonix system snapshot restore node-a.tar.gz --dry-run

  # put the state back (refuses while a container or VM is still running)
  delonix system snapshot restore node-a.tar.gz

  # restore anyway, accepting that the running workloads lose their registry
  delonix system snapshot restore node-a.tar.gz --force

SEE ALSO:
  delonix system snapshot create · delonix container ls · delonix vm ls ·
  delonix secret ls

  delonix › system › snapshot › restore

title: `system thermal` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Thermal governor for Delonix's CPU budget. Runs continuously (see `--once`).

Lowers the budget when the CPU heats up and restores it when it cools down.

Usage: delonix system thermal [OPTIONS]

Options:
      --high <HIGH>
          Temperature (°C) at or above which it cools down
          
          [default: 85]

      --low <LOW>
          Temperature (°C) below which it restores
          
          [default: 70]

      --floor <FLOOR>
          Minimum CPU percentage it drops to
          
          [default: 40]

      --interval <INTERVAL>
          Seconds between readings
          
          [default: 5]

      --once
          One reading and exit (for cron/scripts, instead of the loop)

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # keep the engine's CPU budget in check when the machine heats up
  delonix system thermal

  # one reading and out, for cron
  delonix system thermal --once

  # cool down earlier, and never drop below half the CPU
  delonix system thermal --high 75 --floor 50

title: `vm` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Declarative microVMs: create/ls/start/stop/console.

`describe`/`rm` moved to the generic per-Kind verbs — `delonix describe vm <name>` / `delonix delete vm <name>`.

Usage: delonix vm <COMMAND>

Lifecycle Commands:
  clone            Clone a VM into a new, independent one — its own disk, MAC and UUID (libvirt)
  cloud-init       Change a STOPPED VM's cloud-init — hostname, user, SSH keys — for its next boot
  create           Create (or auto-recover) a VM
  destroy          Destroy VMs and everything they own — provider-side VM, disks, snapshots
  migrate          Move a VM to another `delonix` host — real downtime, no shared storage
  move             Move a VM to another node of its cluster — same VM, same record
  pause            Suspend a running VM's vCPUs — guest memory stays intact, unlike `stop`
  resize           Change a STOPPED VM's vCPUs, memory and/or boot disk size for its next boot
  restart          Stop (if running) then start — always a real reboot, unlike `start`. Same recovered-fields limits as `start`

stdout_head:
Change a STOPPED VM's cloud-init — hostname, user, SSH keys — for its next boot.

Refused while the VM runs or is paused: the guest reads cloud-init at boot. `--ssh-key` REPLACES the keys the VM had; a flag not given keeps its value. On Proxmox the node's config is changed, the cloud-init drive regenerated, and the node's own rendering read back. title: `vm destroy` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Destroy VMs and everything they own — provider-side VM, disks, snapshots.

Unlike `stop` this is not reversible. It goes through the VM's own backend (libvirt, Proxmox, Cloud Hypervisor) and removes the overlay, seed, snapshots, sockets, logs, extra disks and the DHCP reservation. If the provider refuses, the record is kept and the error says why — `--force` drops the local state anyway. Shared volumes are never deleted; extra disks outside the state directory only with `--purge-disks`.

Usage: delonix vm destroy [OPTIONS] <NAMES>...

Arguments:
  <NAMES>...
          

Options:
  -f, --force
          Delete the local state even if the provider refuses the removal

      --purge-disks
          Also delete extra disks that live outside the state directory

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # remove a VM and everything it owns — provider-side VM, overlay, seed,
  # snapshots, sockets, logs, DHCP reservation — and see what was freed
  delonix vm destroy dev

  # several at once, dropping the local state even if the provider refuses the
  # removal
  delonix vm destroy dev1 dev2 --force

  # also delete extra disks that live outside the state directory
  delonix vm destroy dev --purge-disks

title: `vm image convert` responde a --help
expectation: rc=0, ajuda em stdout, stderr vazio
source: clap: toda a folha tem --help; convencao Docker/Podman
stdout_head:
Convert a VM disk between `qcow2` and `raw`.

Flattened (no backing file) either way, ready to boot on either backend (libvirt/QEMU and Cloud Hypervisor already share this same pair of formats; there is no separate "per-hypervisor" format here). `qcow2` is the default — it is the per-VM overlay format.

Usage: delonix vm image convert [OPTIONS] --to <TO> <SOURCE>

Arguments:
  <SOURCE>
          A local VM image name (`vm image ls`) or a literal `.qcow2`/`.raw` path

Options:
      --to <TO>
          Target format

          Possible values:
          - qcow2: QEMU/KVM, libvirt, Cloud Hypervisor — this engine's own two backends
          - raw:   Raw sectors: Proxmox VE (its default for LVM/ZFS/Ceph storage), and the universal fallback anything can read. Not sparse on a filesystem that does not support holes — expect the full virtual size on disk
          - vmdk:  VMware — Workstation, Fusion, ESXi/vSphere
          - vdi:   VirtualBox
          - vhdx:  Hyper-V (Windows 8/2012 and later), and Azure's modern disk format
          - vhd:   Hyper-V's older VHD (`vpc` in qemu-img's own naming). Kept separate from `vhdx` because they are different formats, not spellings — an importer that wants one rejects the other

  -o, --output <OUTPUT>
          Destination file (default: alongside the source, with the new extension)

      --compress
          Compress the output. Only `qcow2` and `vmdk` can — refused for the others rather than handed to `qemu-img` to fail on

  -h, --help
          Print help (see a summary with '-h')

EXAMPLES:
  # hand a Delonix image to VMware
  delonix vm image convert --to vmdk delonix-vm-base:ubuntu-24.04 -o ubuntu-24.04.vmdk

  # raw sectors: Proxmox VE's default on LVM/ZFS/Ceph, and the fallback
  # anything else reads
  delonix vm image convert --to raw proxmox-ve:9.1 -o proxmox-ve.raw

  # Hyper-V and Azure — `vhdx` and `vhd` are different formats, not two
  # spellings of one
  delonix vm image convert --to vhdx delonix-vm-k8s:1.34 -

stdout_head:
Remove a local VM image (its disk and its metadata).

**Refused while a VM still uses it.** A VM created from an image runs on a thin overlay whose backing file IS that image: deleting it out from under a live overlay does not free the VM, it makes it permanently unreadable. `--force` overrides, and says what it is breaking.

Arguments:
  <NAMES>...
          Image name(s), as shown by `vm image ls`
